title: Growing yacon
subtitle: A large South American perennial producing crunchy, sweet root tubers in autumn.
excerpt: Yacon is a tall South American perennial grown for its large, sweet, crunchy tubers harvested in autumn. The flesh tastes of apple or pear and can be eaten raw. It grows quickly once established and reaches 1.5 to 2 m in a good UK summer.
sourceNotes: Cultivation notes from Plants For A Future database (pfaf.org) and Martin Crawford, Creating a Forest Garden (2010). Fructooligosaccharide content from food science literature. UK frost protection guidance widely documented in heritage vegetable sources.

glossaryTerms.definition: The reddish-purple corm-like crown at the top of a yacon root system. The eating tubers are the large storage roots; the propagation crowns are the smaller, firmer structures attached above them. Keep the crowns dry over winter and plant them out in spring to grow the following year's crop.

content.text: Yacon produces two types of underground structure: large, brown storage tubers for eating, and small, reddish
for replanting. The storage tubers have a crisp texture and a sweet, mild flavour similar to water chestnut or Asian pear. They are eaten raw, roasted, or in stir-fries.

Start crowns in pots under glass in April. Keep them warm (above 15 degrees Celsius) until ready to plant out. Plant out in late May once all risk of frost has passed. Space plants 60 to 90 cm apart. They grow fast in warm conditions and will reach 1.5 m by August in a good season.

Harvest after the foliage has been frosted, in October or November. The tops die back and the storage tubers are ready. Dig carefully: the tubers are large and fragile. Remove the eating tubers and set the crowns aside separately.

Store eating tubers in a cool, dark, frost-free place. Their sweetness intensifies after two to four weeks in storage as the fructooligosaccharides convert to simple sugars. Store propagation crowns in barely moist compost at 5 to 10 degrees Celsius until spring.

attrs.title: Yacon and blood sugar
attrs.body: The sweet flavour of yacon comes largely from fructooligosaccharides, a type of fibre that the human body cannot fully digest. This means yacon has a lower glycaemic impact than most sweet root crops. It is sometimes grown specifically by people managing blood sugar levels. It is not a treatment or supplement, but it is low in available sugar compared with parsnip or sweet potato.
